messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 61
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Security Guard
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 76

**Vignette: Moana, 61-year-old Female Security Guard**

Moana has worked security for nearly two decades, first at a shopping centre on the outskirts of Auckland, then at a large hospital complex where she has spent the last eleven years. She is a big woman in the way her family always described with pride — solid, dependable, someone you'd want standing between you and trouble. She took the hospital posting seriously, learning every corridor, every stairwell, every face that came and went. She was good at her job. She believed that.

Three years ago, on a wet Tuesday evening, Moana was responding to a disturbance near the emergency department entrance. A man she had seen before — agitated, possibly in mental health crisis — was blocking the sliding doors. She moved toward him the way she always had, steady and calm, one hand raised, voice low. What happened next took perhaps four seconds. He lurched sideways. She reached out to steady him. Her footing gave way on the wet floor mat. In the fall, her weight came down on him. He struck his head on the concrete kerb. He was hospitalised for six weeks with a traumatic brain injury. He was discharged with permanent cognitive impairment.

Moana remembers the sound. She says it is the first thing that comes back to her — not a crack, exactly, more of a dull, wet thud — and she cannot hear anything strike a hard surface now without her body going rigid. She stood in her kitchen last spring and dropped a ceramic mug, and she was back on that wet mat before the pieces hit the floor, heart slamming, hands shaking, unable to speak for several minutes.

The investigation cleared her. The hospital said it was an accident. Her supervisor told her she had done nothing wrong. She nodded at all of it and did not believe a word. In her mind, the sequence replays differently than the CCTV footage she was shown. In her version, she moved too fast. She should have waited. She should have known the floor was wet. She had been in that entrance a thousand times and she should have known.

She returned to work after six weeks because she did not know what else to do with herself. She is single, her children are grown and live in Australia, and the job has always been her structure. But she is not the same person who walks those corridors now. She avoids the emergency entrance entirely, rerouting her patrols through a longer path that takes her past the oncology ward. Her colleagues have noticed she no longer responds to calls near the main doors; she gives vague reasons and no one pushes her. She sleeps perhaps four hours a night, waking around two in the morning with her chest tight and the image of him falling already waiting for her. She lies in the dark and runs through every decision she made that evening.

She has stopped attending her church, where she was once a regular and a reader at services. She tells herself she is tired on Sundays, but the truth is she does not feel she belongs among people who are trying to be good. She has grown quieter at family video calls, offering less, asking more questions about the grandchildren so no one turns the conversation back to her. When her daughter asked recently if she was all right, Moana said she was just getting older.

What she carries is a particular kind of guilt that has calcified into something she experiences as fact — not that she made a mistake, but that she is the kind of person who destroys others. She is watchful to the point of exhaustion at work, scanning every surface, every posture, every potential hazard, convinced that her own body is the most dangerous thing in any room she enters. The pride she once felt in being solid and dependable has curdled into a vigilance she cannot turn off, and she is very, very tired.
